newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-JUVENTUS COULD BECOME WANDERERS OF ITALY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JUVENTUS COULD BECOME WANDERERS OF ITALY.

text.p: European Cup holders Juventus and Ajax, the Dutch team the Italians prised the title from last year, will meet at Turin's Delle Alpi stadium next month fighting for a place in the Munich final.
For once, the cavernous and unpopular ground may see something close to a capacity crowd.

The match could also, if some reports are to be believed, be the last time Juventus appear there in a European club competition before beginning a new life on the road just when the "Old Lady" is celebrating her 100th anniversary.

"Maybe it was the penultimate cup tie in the scandal-stadium," declared the local Tuttosport daily newspaper on Thursday in a headline over an article highlighting the empty stands, poor lighting and rough pitch.

The runaway Italian league leaders are locked in long-standing talks with the city council over the lease, shared with serie B club Torino, on a stadium that was completed only seven years ago for the 1990 World Cup.
Juventus, while giving clear signs that they want to stay, have threatened to leave the city of their birth.
They have made the threat before, only to come to a compromise, but this time it seems less empty.
A scan of the terraces during Wednesday's quarter-final against Norway's Rosenbborg, won 2-0 by the Italians, suggested that the exodus would not upset too many fans.
The futuristic stadium, with a rarely-used running track distancing the pitch from the stands and making viewing difficult, has never been a popular venue.
It has been called at various times a cathedral in the desert, a refrigerator and a spaceship.
Among the banners displayed were "Juventus fans Grenoble," "Taranto presente" and "Cervinia presente" -- towns in France, the southernmost heel of Italy and the far north.

The maintenance costs at the delle Alpi are huge, like the stadium whose 69,000 seats are rarely filled. Juventus have 28,000 season ticket holders, with two thirds coming from outside the city, Torino just 8,000.
"Turin has created a monster," declared the daily Gazzetta dello Sport in a recent editorial.

Unlike the more advanced English soccer clubs, with their stock listings, merchandising and multi-purpose stadiums, Juventus and Torino have little say in the city-owned delle Alpi, which is used barely more than once a week.

Juventus, with a record 23 league championships and more silverware than any other Italian club, have been looking enviously at the new riches flooding into less successful clubs abroad and do not want to be left behind.

Negotiations are underway with the outgoing council for their old Comunale stadium to be handed over to the club for development into a state-of-the-art ground, allowing Juventus to control fully the advertising income.

The project may well come to fruition but before that, the Delle Alpi rent problem, which also involves a third party in the form of a private company with the advertising and administrative rights, has still to be resolved.
The difficulties have festered for years.
In May 1995, Juventus played a UEFA Cup semifinal in Milan in protest and threatened to leave Turin the following season unless a more favourable deal was forthcoming.
A contract was reportedly signed with Bologna allowing Juventus to play at the Dall'Ara stadium that season but in the end a temporary deal was found to keep them at home.

This season, Juventus played their European Supercup final against Paris St Germain in Palermo and have reportedly agreed with Reggiana to play league matches there. Cup ties would be moved to Milan's San Siro stadium.
Unless, of course, a last-minute solution is reached.
